newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Saudi scoops up French crown jewels, other gems.
newsitem.headline: Saudi scoops up French crown jewels, other gems.

text.p: A Saudi collector who already owns the most expensive diamond sold at auction paid 1.38 million swiss francs ($996,000) on Wednesday for what could be the last French crown jewels to come on the market, Sotheby's said.
Ahmed Fitaihi attended the Geneva gem sale and beamed after acquiring the mid-19th century French royal parure sold off by the Comte de Paris, head of the royal house of Orleans.

The set, by the royal Parisian jeweller Bapst, comprising a tiara, matching earrings, brooches, corsage ornament and centre plaque of a bracelet, belonged to Queen Marie-Amelie of France (1782-1866), wife of King Louis-Philippe d'Orleans.
Fitaihi also grabbed the most valuable lot at Sotheby's gem sale, a pear-shaped blue diamond ring weighing 5.07 carats for 3.08 million swiss francs ($2.2 million).

A major player in the international jewellery auction market, two years ago he bought a 100.1 carat diamond for $16.5 million. The pear-shaped stone, which he named "The Star of the Season", still holds the world record even though it is the third largest (eds: correct) diamond to have been auctioned.

Fitaihi, who owns department stores in Riyadh and his home base of Jeddah, on Wednesday also paid nearly 500,000 swiss francs ($359,190) for a stunning diamond tiara made by the jeweller Cartier in 1920, one of the evening's main lots.
"I got everything I wanted," Fitaihi, white praying beads in hand, told Reuters. "I'll keep it for my private collection."

Sotheby's said that jewels totalling 30 million swiss francs ($21.7 million) were sold at its spring sale on Wednesday. Christie's major gem sale on Tuesday netted 35 million swiss francs ($24.9 million), but lacked pieces of royal provenance.
More than 80 lots of silver and jewellery belonging to the heir of the German Imperial and Royal Prussian House earned $439,571 or nearly double Sotheby's pre-sale estimate.
The 30 jewels belonged to Princess Kira of Prussia, Grand Duchess of Russia, a great grand-daughter of both Queen Victoria and the Russian Tsar Alexander II.

Her husband, Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia died three years ago and his grandson and heir, Prince George Friedrich von Preussen, said in a statement after the sale: "The proceeds will help with the restructuring of the family's holdings."
David Bennett, head of Sotheby's jewellery department who conducted the sale, said: "We were very pleased to have pieces from two royal collections in the sale. That is very rare.
"It is interesting that the parure has passed into private hands after 130 years. It may be the last piece of French royal jewellery to appear on the market," he added.
The French parure had been estimated at about $1,000,000.

The last time a similar French royal tiara was sold, in November 1992 when Germany's Princess Gloria von Thurn and Taxis sold off family jewels and silver, the privately-financed "Friends of the Louvre" bought it for the Paris museum.
That historic tiara, ordered by French Emperor Napoleon III for Eugenie on their wedding, went for $590,000.
Bennett, asked about the apparent lack of museum interest in the Queen Marie-Amelie set, replied: "The Louvre clearly has the other half of the parure and probably that is sufficient."
Regarding Fitaihi, Bennett said: "These three lots are the lots he is prepared to acknowledge having bought."

A fancy deep blue diamond ring weighing 5.3 carats went for just over two million swiss francs ($1.47 million), the second most valuable lot of the night. A vivid purplish pink diamond ring -- which Bennett described as "bubble-gum pink" -- went for 1.76 million swiss francs ($1.27 million) to a telephone bidder.
"The diamond market is strong in general, and the market for coloured diamonds is quite strong," he said.
